title: Thermodynamic Concentration Inequalities: Controlling Uncertainty in Finite-Time and Small-Sample Thermodynamic Inference
abstract: We derive nonasymptotic upper bounds on the probability that a generalized current of a geometrically ergodic diffusion observed for any amount of time, or its sample mean over any arbitrary sample size, deviates from the stationary mean by more than any given amount. The concentration-of-measure behavior of generalized currents is universally governed by the relaxation time of the underlying dynamics, the locally observed dissipation rate, and the intrinsic local fluctuations of the observable. We uncover stark qualitative and quantitative differences in fluctuations in and out of thermodynamic equilibrium. We further obtain refined inverse thermodynamic uncertainty relations, bounding the variance of generalized currents from above. We construct nonasymptotic confidence intervals for controlling uncertainty in thermodynamic inference from small data, i.e., from short trajectories and small samples, and provide the first quantitative answer to when a trajectory is sufficiently long and a sample is sufficiently large. As an illustration, we apply our results to currents observed on a two-dimensional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process in and out of equilibrium and show how they can be used to rigorously detect broken detailed balance.
summary: This paper develops advanced concentration inequalities to provide rigorous, nonasymptotic bounds on the uncertainty when estimating thermodynamic quantities from limited experimental data. By analyzing generalized currents, the authors quantify the required observation time and sample size needed to distinguish between equilibrium and non-equilibrium states. This offers a powerful theoretical framework for modern stochastic thermodynamics and data-driven physics.
main_problem: The paper derives nonasymptotic concentration inequalities to rigorously control the uncertainty associated with estimating thermodynamic quantities from finite-time or small-sample stochastic trajectories.
main_result: It establishes refined inverse thermodynamic uncertainty relations (iTUR) and provides explicit confidence intervals, quantifying how observation time and sample size must scale to achieve a desired accuracy, especially highlighting differences between equilibrium and non-equilibrium dynamics.
method: The methodology relies on deriving concentration bounds (e.g., Cramér-Chernoff approach) for generalized currents and their sample means, extending techniques from stochastic processes theory to finite-data inference.
model_or_system: The analysis is performed on geometrically ergodic, time-homogeneous stochastic processes governed by overdamped Langevin equations on a continuous state space. The focus is on the dynamics' ability to relax to a stationary measure.
key_observables: Generalized current ($	ext{J}_t$), sample mean ($ ar{	ext{J}}_{n,t}$), local steady-state entropy production rate ($\Sigma_{loc}$), and the overall entropy production rate ($\Sigma_U$).
important_parameters: Relaxation time, spectral gap ($\lambda_{	ext{gap}}$), dissipation rate, and the ratio $\Sigma_U/\lambda_{	ext{gap}}$ which quantifies the deviation from equilibrium.
main_assumptions: The dynamics are assumed to be geometrically ergodic, and the derivations rely on bounding moment-generating functions and utilizing properties of the underlying Markovian process.
figures_summary: The notes do not provide a summary of figures, but they detail the mathematical forms of the concentration inequalities and the dependence of the required observation time/sample size on the dissipation factor.
paper_structure: The paper builds from deriving concentration inequalities for the generalized current in finite time, extends these bounds to the sample mean over multiple independent paths, and culminates in deriving refined uncertainty relations and practical bounds for minimal observation time and sample size.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous, quantitative tools for analyzing non-equilibrium steady states, which is crucial for understanding energy dissipation and fluctuation theorems in complex physical systems, bridging statistical mechanics with data science.
